title: PhD thesis
text:
Context
This thesis is part of Work Package 4 of the ANR-RHU EndoVx project. Its purpose is the numerical simulation of 3D-printed models replicating an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), with the goal of developing surgical simulators for training and fast rehearsal of operations.
During endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR), guides are introduced into the anatomy, which produces complex loads at varying locations. Simulating every possible loading position with standard finite elements would be far too slow for a simulator.

title: PhD thesis
text:
Approach: Proper Generalised Decomposition
To address this, the thesis uses reduced-order modelling (ROM), specifically the Proper Generalised Decomposition (PGD). PGD is an a priori ROM technique: it separates variables in the solution, so that complex parametric problems are solved once instead of repeating computations over time or parameter ranges. Here, the extra parameter is the loading position.
Introductory results are first presented in 1D and 2D for a linear elastic material.

title: PhD thesis
text:
Extending PGD to hyperelasticity
The main goal is to extend the method to a hyperelastic material model, which is consistent with the models used for biological tissues and with most of the 3D-printing materials simulated. A hyperelastic material is characterised by a strain energy density function and shows non-linear elastic behaviour. The thesis uses the Saint-Venant–Kirchhoff model: despite known limitations, it is sufficient for this type of work as long as strains stay reasonable. Stress and strain are linked linearly, but strain and displacement follow a non-linear relationship in the finite-strain framework.
Hyperelasticity introduces terms of various orders of non-linearity in the PGD weak form. Handling them requires:

an incremental formulation, treating the full load as a sequence of loading steps, with PGD performed successively on each increment;
a suitable linearisation strategy to compute the PGD solution.

title: PhD thesis
text:
Main contribution: linearisation strategies
The main contribution is the application of a linearisation strategy previously used for other forms of non-linearity. It reduces higher-order terms to first order by introducing a known approximation, and the central question is what this approximation is built from:

Explicit approximation

uses the solution known from the previous modes.

Implicit approximation

adds the last known solution from the computation of the current mode, i.e. performs the linearisation inside the fixed-point loop rather than in the outer PGD loop. More accurate, but more expensive.

Mixed strategy

applies the implicit approximation to some modes only, to keep the cost down. In practice, the first two modes of each increment are computed implicitly and the rest explicitly.

title: PhD thesis
text:
Results
The strategies are compared in 1D and 2D, on a simple rectangular domain and on a more complex Y-shaped domain, and the advantages and drawbacks of each are analysed. The implicit and mixed strategies give good results for third-order computations without requiring small loading increments, while the performance of the other strategies and orders varies from case to case.
The thesis also covers numerical aspects of implementing the method, and briefly explores another PGD decomposition that uses the loading amplitude as the extra parameter, instead of or combined with the loading position.

Postdoctoral researcher · Helmholtz-Zentrum Hereon

I am a postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Material Systems Modeling of the Helmholtz-Zentrum Hereon (Hamburg area, Germany), working in computational mechanics.
I completed my PhD in Computational Mechanics at Université Paris-Saclay in July 2026, at the Laboratoire de Mécanique Paris-Saclay (LMPS), under the supervision of Bing Tie and Andrea Barbarulo. My thesis developed hyperelastic reduced-order models based on the Proper Generalised Decomposition (PGD), for biomimetic material applications such as 3D printing patient-specific aneurysmal aortic models.
